No eclipse, dust, spot or pulsation model gives stepwise, achromatic, permanent dimming of a dwarf; Gaia epoch-calibration offsets are the main alternative but would not be monotonic in three bands plus W1.

discriminating_test: A single low-resolution optical spectrum (or archival spectroscopic/quasar-catalogue cross-match) to check for broad redshifted emission lines; failing that, ZTF g/r light curves after Gaia to see whether the variation continues as a red-noise random walk rather than a one-way fade.

The source is faint (G 19.8), blue (BP-RP 0.6), at high galactic latitude with no measurable parallax and a clean single-source astrometric fit, and its WISE colours are AGN-like (W1-W2 = 1.4, W2-W3 = 3.4, W3-W4 = 2.8). The G fade is smooth (abbe 0.13), agrees between both fields of view, and flattens or reverses at the end. NEOWISE W1 declines more weakly and with a delay, then rebrightens years later, as a dust-torus echo of a varying central source would. BP/RP are too noisy to constrain colour.

discriminating_test: A single low-resolution optical spectrum (or archival spectroscopic/quasar-catalogue cross-match): broad redshifted emission lines confirm an AGN, while stellar absorption lines at zero redshift or a significant proper motion would rule it out.

explanation: Most probably a quasar/AGN, not a star. WISE colours W1-W2 = 1.0 and W2-W3 = 2.6 sit in the AGN locus; the source is faint (G 19.8), blue (BP-RP 0.55), at high galactic latitude with an insignificant parallax. The smooth 42% G fade over 921 d, seen in both fields of view, is ordinary accretion-disk stochastic variability: ZTF g and r later show the same source wandering and rebrightening by 30-50% over seasons, with no fixed period. The weak mid-infrared response fits a lagged, smoothed dust torus rather than grey occultation. BP and RP are too noisy to constrain colour.

discriminating_test: A few nights of continuous ground-based photometry (or any dense archival survey light curve of this star) searched for strictly periodic, hours-long ~15-18% eclipses; equivalently, check the Gaia per-CCD fluxes, scan angles and window/across-scan positions of the three fov-1 dip transits. Periodic recurrence confirms an eclipsing binary; none, with anomalous window positions, points to instrumental flux loss.

A third dip (0.952 at t=133.34) recovers within 106 min. All three dips appear in G, BP and RP together and are roughly grey, on an otherwise quiet star. This is what a sparsely sampled detached eclipsing binary with hours-long eclipses looks like; the 45.7 d period is a loose alias. Caveat: all three dips are in field of view 1 with no fov-2 confirmation, so a per-transit flux loss remains possible.

discriminating_test: Independent multi-band ground-based forced photometry (for example ATLAS or Pan-STARRS epochs) over t=540-900 on the packet clock: a 2-3% dimming seen there with BP-like depth larger than RP-like depth supports spots or dust, a grey one supports an occulter, and none at all points to a Gaia G-only artefact. The same Gaia transits of neighbouring stars of similar magnitude would give the instrumental check at no cost.

explanation: Most probable: a spot-coverage episode on a K dwarf. G drops ~2.5% for ~230 d in both fields of view (11 consecutive epochs, 6 visits), so not a single-transit or field-of-view artefact; excess factor, ruwe and multi-peak fraction are nominal, so no blend. A normal visit at t=786 between dim visits at 772 and 832, and a 1% recovery within 6 d (832 to 838), suggest modulated intrinsic variability rather than one smooth occultation. Confidence is low: the star is otherwise photon-noise quiet, BP/RP cannot confirm the dip or its colour (RP shows none), and no infrared or second survey exists, so a tenuous extended occulter, a G-only calibration residual, or a non-natural injected episode remain open.

discriminating_test: Archival two-band ground photometry covering 2015-2019 (ATLAS c/o, ASAS-SN, Pan-STARRS) on one zero point: whether the star kept fading to about 2% in early 2018 and recovered by 2019, and whether the blue band changed about 1.4-1.7 times more than the red; a real, chromatic, recovering dip rules out Gaia calibration and grey blocking, while a flat curve points to an instrumental or injected Gaia-only signal.

explanation: Smooth ~0.9% G fade (1.002 to 0.993) beginning between days 410 and 536 and persisting to the last Gaia visit, identical in both fields of view, on a star otherwise quiet at the 0.1% level. RP dims about half as much as G and BP about as much or more: mildly chromatic rather than grey; NEOWISE cannot discriminate. ZTF is 0.5-2% fainter in 2018 than in 2019-2025, hinting the dimming was real and recovered. Most probable: slow change of spot coverage or temperature on a slowly rotating, reddened subgiant or giant; circumstellar dust or residual Gaia calibration drift remain viable. The shallow depth leaves classes poorly separated.
